item.title: After Two Decades, U.S. Forces Leave Iraq to an Uncertain Future
item.description: Some Iraqis are celebrating the end of an American military presence that unleashed waves of bloodshed. Others fear what happens next for their country, trapped between Washington and Tehran.
item.dc:creator: Erika Solomon, Falih Hassan and Eric Schmitt
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:credit: Zaid Al-Obeidi/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: A giant Iraqi flag hung from the Great Mosque of al-Nuri in Mosul’s old city on Tuesday. With the end of Operation Inherent Resolve, the last of the 2,500 U.S. forces stationed in Iraq this year are now gone.

item.title: American Forces Withdraw From Iraq 23 Years After Invading
item.description: The Americans did not understand the country when they invaded in 2003. Over a correspondent’s many trips there, it was not clear that this ever changed much.
item.dc:creator: Alissa J. Rubin
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces
item.media:credit: Tyler Hicks/The New York Times
item.media:description: In March 2003, a statue of Saddam Hussein was still standing near a communications center in Baghdad that had been bombed two days earlier. A month later, the statue would be downed as well.

item.title: U.S. Withdraws From Iraq After Two Decades, and Trump Tells A.I. Giants to Police Themselves
item.description: Plus, the nepo babies take Fat Bear Week.
item.dc:creator: Tracy Mumford, Will Jarvis, Margaret Kadifa, Jake Lucas, Ian Stewart, Erika Solomon and Sheera Frenkel
item.category: United States Defense and Military Forces

item.title: How Meta Uses A.I. Data Centers to Avoid Billions in Federal Taxes
item.description: Meta is exploiting a lucrative tax break intended to support research and experimentation. Its own accountants say the gambit is risky.
item.dc:creator: Kashmir Hill, Jesse Drucker, Eli Tan and Mike Isaac
item.media:credit: Illustration by Joan Wong; Photographs by Jason Henry for The New York Times, Mike Stewart/Associated Press, Getty Images

item.title: DeepSeek and Huawei Target a Key Source of Nvidia’s A.I. Dominance
item.description: In China’s push for self-reliance in artificial intelligence, DeepSeek and Huawei have teamed up to develop software tools for advanced chips.
item.dc:creator: Steve Lohr
item.media:credit: Jade Gao/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: DeepSeek’s headquarters in Hangzhou, China. The company announced a partnership with Huawei for software tools.

item.title: Troubles at Situational Awareness Point to Record Stock Market Leverage
item.description: A meltdown at Situational Awareness, an A.I.-focused investment firm, is raising tough questions about the Wall Street banks that lent billions to the upstart firm.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Goldstein and Rob Copeland
item.media:credit: Nicholas Albrecht for The New York Times
item.media:description: Big banks lent Leopold Aschenbrenner’s firm billions to invest in the artificial intelligence boom. Then the firm had a meltdown.

item.title: Hispanic Voters on the Texas Border Have Soured on Trump
item.description: In 2024, these voters were an essential part of the winning Republican coalition. Now, many feel abandoned and furious, complicating the party’s chances in November.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Medina and Edgar Sandoval
item.media:credit: Tamir Kalifa for The New York Times

item.title: Ken Paxton, G.O.P. Nominee in Texas, Privately Said Trump’s Convention Hurt Him
item.description: Ken Paxton, one of the party’s top Senate candidates and a Trump loyalist, said that “everybody’s numbers dropped” after the event, according to audio obtained by The Times.
item.dc:creator: Theodore Schleifer
item.media:credit: Shelby Tauber for The New York Times
item.media:description: Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, as President Trump addressed him during the second day of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas this month.

item.title: As Violence Falls, Crime Isn’t Paying as a Republican Line of Attack
item.description: Across the country, especially in the North Carolina Senate race, Republicans have charged opponents with being soft on crime, even as President Trump brags over plunging crime rates.
item.dc:creator: Shaila Dewan
item.media:credit: Kate Medley for The New York Times
item.media:description: Roy Cooper, the Democratic candidate for Senate in North Carolina, at a rally in Durham, N.C.

item.title: Los Angeles Mayoral Candidates Vie for Undecided Voters
item.description: Mayor Karen Bass and her onetime ally, Nithya Raman, made their case to voters with just five weeks left until the election.
item.dc:creator: Shawn Hubler
item.media:credit: Jae C. Hong/Associated Press

item.title: D.A. in Cornell Case Hopes to Speak to Accuser as He Weighs New Evidence
item.description: District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said a woman’s report to police in 2024 saying she had been raped at a fraternity did not support a criminal case. But he said he is now reaching out to her.
item.dc:creator: Hurubie Meko
item.media:credit: Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office
item.media:description: Matthew Van Houten, district attorney for Tompkins County, N.Y., said some new evidence is emerging in an allegation of rape at Cornell University.

item.title: Cornell University Rape Investigation: What We Know
item.description: Prosecutors have reopened the case of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted on campus in 2024. The woman’s lawsuit brought renewed pressure to reopen the investigation.
item.dc:creator: Sharon Otterman
item.media:credit: Heather Ainsworth for The New York Times
item.media:description: Students walk past the now shuttered Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y.

item.title: Can President Trump Demolish the Kennedy Center? Experts Say Not Easily.
item.description: The president has entertained the idea of tearing down the performing arts venue. Analysts say any plan would face multiple daunting challenges.
item.dc:creator: Julia Jacobs
item.category: Kennedy, John F, Center for the Performing Arts
item.media:credit: Kenny Holston/The New York Times
item.media:description: An image of President Trump reviewing a poster that appears to relate to the demolition of the Kennedy Center has led to heightened concerns he might move to destroy the performing arts venue.

item.title: Trump’s New Tariffs Face a Familiar Court Challenge
item.description: For the third time in less than two years, the Trump administration is set to return to court on Wednesday to defend its power to wage a punishing global trade war.
item.dc:creator: Tony Romm
item.media:credit: Doug Mills/The New York Times
item.media:description: Despite two years of economic shocks and uncertainty, President Trump still sees sky-high tariffs as potent economic tools for his policies.

item.title: How Ukraine’s Naval Drones Are Remaking War at Sea
item.description: They began as modified motorboats. Now, Ukrainian sea drones act as miniature aircraft carriers, and other countries want in.
item.dc:creator: Maria Varenikova and Nicholas Kulish
item.media:credit: Maria Varenikova/The New York Times
item.media:description: A Magura sea drone at a test site in central Ukraine in June.

item.title: New Cancer Drugs Are Revolutionary. Why Don’t More Patients Get Them?
item.description: Targeted gene therapies are highly effective at stopping cancers, but the very abundance of the treatments, plus cost and sluggish change, are hindering access.
item.dc:creator: Gina Kolata
item.media:credit: Emily Elconin for The New York Times
item.media:description: When John Ebers, a commercial beekeeper in Comstock Park, Mich., was diagnosed with Stage 3 colorectal cancer, he was not given the option of genetic testing, which could have revealed if there were drugs that could attack his cancer.

item.title: Jack Smith Defends Trump Charges as Senator’s Perjury Claim Falls Apart
item.description: A Republican eager to prove the former special counsel was dishonest appeared to instead demonstrate his own confusion over basic facts.
item.dc:creator: Devlin Barrett and Charlie Savage

item.title: As E-Bikes and Scooters Surge on New York Streets, So Do Fatal Crashes
item.description: More than two dozen people have died in crashes involving electric bikes and scooters in New York City this year. Officials are moving to address a growing safety crisis.
item.dc:creator: Emma G. Fitzsimmons
item.media:credit: Hilary Swift for The New York Times
item.media:description: The Manhattan intersection where a 15-year-old girl riding an electric Citi Bike was struck and killed by a truck this month.

item.title: After Fatal Crashes, N.Y.C. Lawmakers Seek to Regulate E-Bikes
item.description: Lawmakers are expected on Wednesday to discuss a raft of proposals to regulate the use of electric bikes and scooters, after a series of fatal crashes.
item.dc:creator: Stefanos Chen
item.media:credit: Sasha Maslov for The New York Times
item.media:description: Of the 20 cyclists that have died this year, most were riding electric bikes, some of which can far exceed the speed limit on these devices.

item.media:description: The donation from the hedge fund executive Kenneth C. Griffin is more than the record $2 billion gift given to Oregon Health and Science University recently.

item.title: In Fractious France, Politicians Agree on One Thing: Pope Leo Was a Hit
item.description: In a four-day visit, Pope Leo XIV won praise across the political spectrum, even from its most avowedly secular figures.
item.dc:creator: Mark Landler and Motoko Rich
item.media:credit: Alberto Pizzoli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: Pope Leo XIV, riding down Avenue des Champs-Élysées on Saturday. The crowds were striking display of reverence from a proudly secular country.
